<!-- ENGINEER-PROF: Same STAT 151 concern as probability/01 — this chapter covers MLE, hypothesis testing, regression, and ANOVA at a level well beyond STAT 151 content. STAT 265 or equivalent engineering-statistics course is a more accurate mapping. -->

A production line fills bottles to a stated volume. A sample of 25
bottles shows a mean fill of 497 mL against a target of 500 mL.
Is that a real problem, or just expected random variation? You need
a principled way to decide.

A new catalyst cuts reaction time in a lab test. But the test used
only eight runs. How confident are you that the effect is real and
not noise?

You have data. The question is what the data can actually tell you —
and, just as importantly, what it cannot.

## Point estimation

You observe $n$ independent realisations $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ from
a distribution that has an unknown parameter $\theta$ — a proportion, a
rate, a mean. A **point estimate** $\hat{\theta}$ — read "theta-hat" —
is a single number computed from the sample to serve as your best guess
at $\theta$.

The most systematic method for finding point estimates is **maximum
likelihood estimation (MLE)**: choose the value of $\theta$ that makes
the observed data most probable.

### Setting up the likelihood

If the $x_i$ are i.i.d. (independent, identically distributed) from a
distribution with density (or mass function) $f(x; \theta)$, the
**likelihood** is the joint probability of the observed data, viewed as
a function of $\theta$:

<!-- STUDENT: "i.i.d." is used here without being expanded at first use in this chapter. Readers coming to this chapter without having read Vol 7 Ch 1 recently may not recall the abbreviation. A parenthetical "(independent, identically distributed)" on first use costs nothing. -->

$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i; \theta)$$

Read this as: the product, over all $n$ observations, of the density
evaluated at each $x_i$. The MLE is the $\theta$ that maximises this.

Products are hard to differentiate. Take the natural log — it's
monotone, so the maximum is preserved. The **log-likelihood** is:

$$\ell(\theta) = \log L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(x_i;\theta)$$

Read "$\ell(\theta)$" as "ell of theta". Now differentiate and set equal
to zero.

### MLE for the Bernoulli distribution

Let $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$: each observation is 1 (success) or
0 (failure), with unknown success probability $p$. Then
$f(x; p) = p^x (1-p)^{1-x}$, so:

For $x=1$, this gives $f(1;p)=p$. For $x=0$, it gives
$f(0;p)=1-p$. So this compact formula is just the Bernoulli mass function
written in one line.

<!-- STUDENT: The Bernoulli mass function f(x;p) = p^x (1−p)^(1−x) is presented without explanation. A reader who saw the Bernoulli defined in Ch 1 as P(X=1)=p, P(X=0)=1−p may not immediately see that this formula is the same thing written compactly. Plugging in x=0 and x=1 to verify would take one line and would make the derivation that follows self-contained. -->

$$\ell(p) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ x_i \log p + (1-x_i)\log(1-p) \right]
= \left(\sum x_i\right)\log p + \left(n - \sum x_i\right)\log(1-p)$$

Let $S = \sum x_i$ (the count of successes). Differentiate with respect
to $p$ and set to zero:

$$\frac{d\ell}{dp} = \frac{S}{p} - \frac{n - S}{1-p} = 0$$

Multiply through by $p(1-p)$:

$$S(1-p) - (n-S)p = 0 \implies S - Sp - np + Sp = 0 \implies S = np$$

$$\boxed{\hat{p} = \frac{S}{n} = \bar{X}}$$

The MLE is the sample proportion. This confirms the intuition.
This means maximum likelihood recovers the estimate you would probably guess
from common sense: the best estimate of a success probability is the observed
fraction of successes.

### MLE for the Exponential distribution

Let $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$: density $f(x;\lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$
for $x \geq 0$. The log-likelihood is:

$$\ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\log\lambda - \lambda x_i\right]
= n\log\lambda - \lambda \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$$

Differentiate and set to zero:

$$\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = \frac{n}{\lambda} - \sum x_i = 0
\implies \lambda = \frac{n}{\sum x_i}$$

$$\boxed{\hat{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\bar{X}}}$$

The MLE of the rate is the reciprocal of the sample mean. If the mean
lifetime in the sample is 5 hours, you estimate the failure rate as 0.2
failures per hour.

### Unbiasedness and consistency

A point estimate is **unbiased** if $E[\hat{\theta}] = \theta$ — the
estimate is correct on average. The sample mean $\bar{X}$ is unbiased
for $\mu$; the sample variance $s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2$
is unbiased for $\sigma^2$ (the $n-1$ denominator matters here — the
$n$ version is biased). The reason is that $\bar{X}$ is estimated from
the same data: once the mean is fixed, only $n-1$ of the deviations
$(X_i - \bar{X})$ are free to vary, so the sum of squared deviations
has $n-1$ degrees of freedom, not $n$.

<!-- STUDENT: The n−1 denominator is flagged as important but the reason is not given, not even in summary form. An engineering student who has used a calculator or spreadsheet will have seen both n and n−1 sample variance formulas and wondered why. The explanation — that using n underestimates σ² because x̄ is estimated from the same data, consuming one degree of freedom — is a single sentence. Without it, "the n−1 denominator matters" is an instruction without a reason. -->

An estimate is **consistent** if $\hat{\theta} \to \theta$ in probability
as $n \to \infty$ — more data drives the estimate to the truth. The MLE
is consistent under mild regularity conditions.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Why MLE works**

The likelihood is the probability of your data given $\theta$. Maximising
it over $\theta$ answers: "which parameter value would make this data least
surprising?" That question has a principled answer even when no other
method is obvious — just write down the distribution, form the product,
and differentiate.
:::

## Confidence intervals

A point estimate is a single number. It conceals the uncertainty. A
**confidence interval** (CI) pairs the estimate with a margin that
quantifies how much the estimate might be off.

### The problem with small samples

If $\sigma$ (the population standard deviation) were known, the sampling
distribution of $\bar{X}$ is exactly $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$, and you could
build an interval using the standard normal $z$-distribution. But $\sigma$
is almost never known — you estimate it from the sample as $s$. When $n$
is small, this extra source of uncertainty matters.

Student's $t$-distribution handles this. The statistic

$$T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}$$

follows a $t$-distribution with $\nu = n-1$ degrees of freedom.

The name "Student" comes from a pseudonym used by William Gosset, a statistician
working for Guinness who published under that pen name.

<!-- STUDENT: The name "Student's t-distribution" will prompt most readers to wonder who "Student" is — the name is peculiar enough to be distracting. Even a single parenthetical noting it is a pseudonym (William Gosset, Guinness brewery, early 1900s) would satisfy the curiosity and let the reader move on. Also, the notation ν = n−1 for degrees of freedom is introduced here but ν does not appear in notation_introduced. --> Read
"$s/\sqrt{n}$" as the **standard error of the mean** — the typical spread
of sample means around the true mean. The $t$-distribution looks like the
standard normal but with heavier tails; as $\nu \to \infty$ it converges
to the normal.

### Constructing a 95% CI for $\mu$

Let $t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ be the upper $\alpha/2$ critical value of the
$t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom — the value such that
$P(T > t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}) = \alpha/2$. For a 95% CI, $\alpha = 0.05$.

<!-- STUDENT: The step "inverting |T| ≤ t_{α/2, n−1}" is not shown. For a reader seeing CI derivation for the first time, the pivot from |T| ≤ critical value to x̄ ± t·s/√n requires two algebraic moves (substituting T, then rearranging the absolute value). The result is a formula that appears without visible connection to the inequality that preceded it. Showing the inversion once — even in a compressed form — would make the worked example fully self-contained. -->

Inverting $|T| \leq t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ gives the interval. Substituting
$T = (\bar{X} - \mu)/(s/\sqrt{n})$ and expanding the absolute value:

$$-t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1} \leq \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \leq t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$$

Multiply through by $s/\sqrt{n}$ and rearrange to isolate $\mu$:

$$\bar{X} - t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\cdot\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
  \;\leq\; \mu \;\leq\;
  \bar{X} + t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\cdot\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

Written compactly:

$$\bar{X} \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

This is the 95% confidence interval for $\mu$.
This means a confidence interval is always doing the same structural job:
estimate at the centre, uncertainty as the margin.

**Worked example.** A materials lab measures Young's modulus for 10
specimens of a polymer. The sample mean is $\bar{x} = 3.42$ GPa and the
sample standard deviation is $s = 0.18$ GPa. The $t$-table gives
$t_{0.025,\,9} = 2.262$.

$$\text{CI} = 3.42 \pm 2.262 \times \frac{0.18}{\sqrt{10}}
= 3.42 \pm 2.262 \times 0.0569
= 3.42 \pm 0.129$$

The 95% CI is $(3.29,\; 3.55)$ GPa.

### What a confidence interval means — and what it does not

The 95% CI does **not** mean "there is a 95% probability that $\mu$ lies
in this interval." After the data are observed, $\mu$ is either in the
interval or it isn't — there is no probability involved.

The correct interpretation: if you repeated this experiment many times and
built a 95% CI each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the
true $\mu$. The *procedure* has 95% coverage. Any particular interval is
just one instance of that procedure.

<!-- VIZ: CI simulation — button generates 100 samples from N(μ,1), draws each 95% CI, highlights the ~5 that miss the true mean, counter shows coverage rate -->

## Hypothesis testing

Point estimates and CIs describe what the data show. Hypothesis testing
asks a sharper question: is there enough evidence to reject a specific
claim?

### The framework

The **null hypothesis** $H_0$ is the claim under scrutiny — the default,
conservative position. The **alternative hypothesis** $H_1$ is what you'd
conclude if $H_0$ is implausible given the data.

A **test statistic** is a function of the data whose distribution under
$H_0$ is known. You compute the observed value, then ask: if $H_0$ were
true, how often would you see a value this extreme or more extreme?
That probability is the **p-value**.

If the p-value is below the **significance level** $\alpha$ (typically
0.05), you reject $H_0$.

Two error types:

| | $H_0$ true | $H_0$ false |
|---|---|---|
| Reject $H_0$ | Type I error (false positive), probability $\alpha$ | Correct |
| Fail to reject $H_0$ | Correct | Type II error (false negative), probability $\beta$ |

Choosing $\alpha = 0.05$ means you're willing to falsely reject a true
$H_0$ in 5% of experiments. Reducing $\alpha$ reduces Type I errors but
increases Type II errors. The power of a test is $1 - \beta$ — the
probability of correctly detecting a real effect.

### One-sample $t$-test

**Hypotheses.** You want to test whether a population mean $\mu$ equals
a specified value $\mu_0$:
$$H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \qquad H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0 \quad \text{(two-sided)}$$

**Test statistic.**

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}$$

Under $H_0$ this follows $t_{n-1}$.

**Decision rule.** Reject $H_0$ if $|t| > t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$.

**Worked example.** A valve is designed to open at 200 kPa. Quality
control samples $n = 20$ valves. The sample mean opening pressure is
$\bar{x} = 203.4$ kPa with $s = 5.2$ kPa. Test $H_0: \mu = 200$ at
$\alpha = 0.05$.

$$t = \frac{203.4 - 200}{5.2/\sqrt{20}} = \frac{3.4}{1.163} = 2.923$$

The critical value is $t_{0.025,\,19} = 2.093$. Since $2.923 > 2.093$,
reject $H_0$. There is statistically significant evidence that the mean
opening pressure differs from 200 kPa.

### Two-sample $t$-test

To compare means $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ from two independent populations
(assuming equal variances), form the pooled variance:

$$s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}$$

The test statistic is:

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}}$$

Under $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$, this follows $t_{n_1+n_2-2}$. Reject when
$|t| > t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}$.

Welch's $t$-test removes the equal-variance assumption by adjusting the
degrees of freedom; it's the default in most software. The pooled test is a
little more powerful when equal variances really are plausible, while Welch is
safer when they may not be.

<!-- STUDENT: Welch's test is mentioned as the default in software and then dropped. A reader who uses R, Python, or MATLAB will immediately want to know: if Welch is the default, why was the pooled version just taught? A single sentence explaining the tradeoff — pooled is more powerful when the equal-variance assumption holds; Welch is safer when it might not — would give the reader a decision rule. -->

### $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit

When the data are counts in categories, the $\chi^2$ statistic tests
whether the observed frequencies are consistent with a specified
distribution. For $k$ categories with observed counts $O_i$ and expected
counts $E_i = n p_i$:

$$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}$$

Under $H_0$, this follows approximately $\chi^2_{k-1}$. Reject if
$\chi^2 > \chi^2_{\alpha,\,k-1}$. The rule of thumb $E_i \geq 5$ in
every cell ensures the approximation is reliable.

## Linear regression

Data rarely have a single variable of interest in isolation. Regression
asks how one variable changes with another — and how reliably.

### The model

The **simple linear regression model** is:

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n$$

$Y_i$ is the response (outcome), $x_i$ is the predictor (input),
$\beta_0$ is the **intercept** (read "beta-zero" — the expected response
when $x = 0$), $\beta_1$ is the **slope** (read "beta-one" — the change
in expected response per unit increase in $x$), and $\varepsilon_i$ is
the error term, assumed i.i.d. $N(0, \sigma^2)$.

### OLS estimators

**Ordinary least squares** minimises the **sum of squared residuals**:

$$\text{SS}_{res} = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
= \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i)^2$$

Read "$\text{SS}_{res}$" as "residual sum of squares" — the total vertical
distance squared between the data points and the fitted line.

Differentiate $\text{SS}_{res}$ with respect to $\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$
and set both partial derivatives to zero. This gives the **normal
equations**. Here "normal" means perpendicular or orthogonal, not "normal
distribution":

<!-- STUDENT: The term "normal equations" is introduced here without explanation of why they are called that. The name has nothing to do with the normal distribution; it comes from the geometric concept of orthogonal projection. Engineering students who just spent a chapter on the normal distribution will be confused by the coincidence of terminology. Even a brief note — "the word 'normal' here means perpendicular, not Gaussian" — would prevent a false connection. -->

$$\frac{\partial\,\text{SS}_{res}}{\partial\hat{\beta}_0} = -2\sum(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0$$

$$\frac{\partial\,\text{SS}_{res}}{\partial\hat{\beta}_1} = -2\sum x_i(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0$$

From the first equation: distribute the sum and use $\sum_{i=1}^n 1 = n$:

$$\sum(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0
\implies n\bar{y} - n\hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot n\bar{x} = 0$$

Divide by $n$: $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}$.

<!-- STUDENT: The step from ∂SS/∂β̂₀ = 0 to β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄ is not shown. A new reader asked to verify this would need to distribute the sum, use Σ1 = n, and divide by n. The algebra is short but not obvious. The text jumps from "first equation" to the result. -->

Substituting into the second and solving:

$$\boxed{\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
= \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}$$

$$\boxed{\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}}$$

where $S_{xy} = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})$ and
$S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2$.
This means the fitted line is pinned to the centre of the data cloud at
$(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ and tilts according to how strongly $x$ and $y$ move
together.

### $R^2$ — coefficient of determination

Define the **total sum of squares** $\text{SS}_{tot} = \sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2$
and the **residual sum of squares** $\text{SS}_{res} = \sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$.
The coefficient of determination is:

$$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SS}_{res}}{\text{SS}_{tot}}$$

$R^2 = 1$ means the line passes through every data point. $R^2 = 0$
means the line explains none of the variation — it is no better than
simply predicting $\bar{y}$ for every observation. In simple linear
regression, $R^2 = r^2$ where $r$ is the Pearson correlation coefficient, the
sample analogue of the population correlation $\rho$ from the previous chapter.

<!-- STUDENT: The Pearson correlation coefficient r is introduced here for the first time in this chapter without a formula. In Ch 1, the population correlation was denoted ρ. A reader who noticed that will wonder whether r and ρ are the same concept, and if so, why the symbol changed. A brief note — "r is the sample version of the population correlation ρ from Ch 1" — would close this gap. -->

### $t$-test for $\beta_1$

Under the model assumptions, the standardised slope estimate

$$t = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1 - 0}{s_e / \sqrt{S_{xx}}}$$

follows $t_{n-2}$ under $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$, where
$s_e^2 = \text{SS}_{res}/(n-2)$ is the estimated error variance. The
denominator is $n-2$ rather than $n-1$ because two parameters ($\beta_0$
and $\beta_1$) are estimated from the data, consuming two degrees of
freedom. Reject $H_0$ if $|t| > t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}$. Failing to reject
means there is no statistically significant linear relationship between
$x$ and $Y$.

<!-- STUDENT: The degrees of freedom are n−2 here (not n−1 as in the one-sample t-test). The reason — two parameters β₀ and β₁ are estimated, consuming two degrees of freedom — is not stated. A reader who just learned n−1 for the one-sample case will notice the change and not know why. -->

### Residual analysis

The regression assumptions — linearity, constant variance, normality of
errors, independence — are checked through the residuals
$\hat{\varepsilon}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$.

Plot residuals against fitted values $\hat{y}_i$:

- **Random scatter around zero** — assumptions satisfied.
- **Curved pattern** — linearity is violated; consider a transformation
  or a polynomial term.
- **Fan shape (variance increasing with $\hat{y}_i$)** — heteroscedasticity;
  consider a log or square-root transformation of $Y$.
- **Outliers** — single points far from zero; investigate individually.

A normal Q-Q plot of residuals checks the normality assumption. Points
falling close to the diagonal line support the assumption.

<!-- VIZ: regression explorer — scatter plot of ~20 points, sliders for β₀ and β̂₁, live SSR display, "Fit OLS" button snaps to optimal line, shows R² -->

## One-way ANOVA

When you want to compare means across three or more groups, running
multiple $t$-tests inflates the Type I error rate. One-way ANOVA
(analysis of variance) tests all groups simultaneously.

### The F-test

Suppose you have $k$ groups, with $n_j$ observations in group $j$.
Let $\bar{y}_{j\cdot}$ denote the mean of group $j$ and $\bar{y}$
the overall mean. Define:

$$\text{SS}_{between} = \sum_{j=1}^k n_j (\bar{y}_{j\cdot} - \bar{y})^2
\qquad \text{(variation explained by group membership)}$$

$$\text{SS}_{within} = \sum_{j=1}^k \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_{j\cdot})^2
\qquad \text{(variation within groups)}$$

The **mean squares** are $\text{MS}_{between} = \text{SS}_{between}/(k-1)$
and $\text{MS}_{within} = \text{SS}_{within}/(N-k)$, where $N = \sum n_j$.

The **F-statistic** is:

$$F = \frac{\text{MS}_{between}}{\text{MS}_{within}}$$

Under $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k$, $F$ follows $F_{k-1,\,N-k}$.
Reject $H_0$ if $F > F_{\alpha,\,k-1,\,N-k}$. A large $F$ means
between-group variation is large relative to within-group variation —
the groups genuinely differ.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Why F instead of multiple $t$-tests?**

With $k = 3$ groups, running all pairwise $t$-tests at $\alpha = 0.05$
gives a familywise error rate of approximately $1 - (0.95)^3 \approx 0.14$.
You'd falsely reject a true null about 14% of the time rather than 5%.
ANOVA controls this by testing all groups in a single F-test. If ANOVA
rejects $H_0$, post-hoc pairwise tests (Tukey HSD, Bonferroni) then
identify which groups differ.
:::

**Engineering application.** Three machine settings — A, B, C — produce
polymer film. Quality engineers measure tensile strength (MPa) from five
runs at each setting:

| Setting A | Setting B | Setting C |
|----------:|----------:|----------:|
| 41.2 | 38.5 | 44.1 |
| 40.8 | 39.2 | 43.8 |
| 42.1 | 37.9 | 45.0 |
| 41.5 | 38.8 | 44.3 |
| 40.4 | 39.6 | 43.4 |

Group means: $\bar{y}_{A} = 41.2$, $\bar{y}_{B} = 38.8$,
$\bar{y}_{C} = 44.12$. Overall mean $\bar{y} = 41.37$.

$\text{SS}_{between} = 5(41.2-41.37)^2 + 5(38.8-41.37)^2 + 5(44.12-41.37)^2$
$= 5(0.0289) + 5(6.6049) + 5(7.5625) = 0.1445 + 33.02 + 37.81 = 70.98$

$\text{MS}_{between} = 70.98/2 = 35.49$

Computing $\text{SS}_{within}$ from deviations within each group gives
approximately $4.61$, so $\text{MS}_{within} = 4.61/12 = 0.384$.

$$F = \frac{35.49}{0.384} = 92.4$$

The critical value $F_{0.05,\,2,\,12} = 3.89$. Since $92.4 \gg 3.89$,
reject $H_0$. The machine settings produce significantly different
tensile strengths — the effect is not noise.

## Where this goes

The methods here assume a parametric form for the distributions —
Bernoulli, exponential, normal. **Non-parametric tests** (Wilcoxon,
Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis) make weaker assumptions at the cost of
some power; they become relevant when distributions are heavily skewed
or sample sizes are very small. **Bayesian inference** reframes the
problem entirely: instead of asking "what does the data tell us about
$\theta$?" it asks "given a prior belief about $\theta$ and the data,
what should our updated belief be?" Both extensions build on exactly the
likelihood functions you derived here.

Multiple linear regression extends the single-predictor model to
$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p + \varepsilon$.
The OLS estimator in matrix form is $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}$,
which requires the linear algebra from Volume 7's linear algebra section.
Generalised linear models (GLMs) then extend regression to non-normal
responses — logistic regression for binary outcomes, Poisson regression
for counts — connecting directly to the MLE framework you already have.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Where this shows up**

- **Reliability engineering:** MLE estimates failure rates from
  field data; confidence intervals bound the estimate; hypothesis
  tests determine whether a design change made a difference.
- **Clinical trials:** two-sample $t$-tests compare treatment
  and control groups; sample size is set to achieve target power.
- **Process control:** $t$-tests on subgroup means detect shifts
  in a manufacturing process mean; ANOVA compares multiple line
  configurations simultaneously.
- **Geophysics:** linear regression of seismic travel time against
  distance estimates subsurface velocity; the $t$-test for $\beta_1$
  determines whether the relationship is real.
- **Machine learning:** the OLS solution is closed-form linear
  regression; $R^2$ and residual analysis evaluate model fit before
  any regularisation is added.
:::

## Exercises

These are puzzles. Each has a clean numerical answer. The work is in
setting up the likelihood, test statistic, or normal equations correctly
before computing.

---

**Exercise 1.** An engineer records the time to failure (hours) for
five identical electronic components under accelerated testing:

$$x_1 = 820, \quad x_2 = 1\,040, \quad x_3 = 650, \quad x_4 = 930, \quad x_5 = 760$$

Assuming lifetimes are Exponential($\lambda$), find $\hat{\lambda}$
(the MLE) and its standard error. Use the fact that for the
Exponential MLE, $\text{SE}(\hat{\lambda}) = \hat{\lambda}/\sqrt{n}$.

STUDENT REVIEW
Reviewer: student agent
Layer: engineering
Date: 2026-04-01

VERDICT: READABLE WITH FIXES

SUMMARY
The chapter is dense but coherent. The worked examples are well-chosen and the
steppers are thorough. Ten friction points were found where notation arrives
unannounced, a step is skipped, or a name is used without the context an
engineering student would need. None individually derails the chapter, but
several cluster around the CI derivation and the OLS section, where the reader
is expected to make multiple leaps in quick succession.

ISSUES (in order of appearance)

1. "i.i.d." — MLE setup
   Used without expansion in this chapter. Readers who have not read Ch 1
   recently will not recognise the abbreviation.
   FLAGGED inline.

2. Bernoulli mass function f(x;p) = p^x(1−p)^(1−x) — MLE Bernoulli subsection
   The compact exponent form of the Bernoulli PMF is presented without
   verification that it matches the P(X=1)=p, P(X=0)=1−p definition in Ch 1.
   The derivation that follows depends on this but a reader who has not seen
   this trick before will have to accept it on faith.
   FLAGGED inline.

3. n−1 denominator in sample variance — Unbiasedness paragraph
   The chapter flags the n−1 denominator as important but gives no reason.
   This is one of the most commonly misunderstood facts in introductory
   statistics and deserves at minimum a one-sentence explanation about
   degrees of freedom.
   FLAGGED inline.

4. "Student's" — t-distribution
   The proper name "Student's t-distribution" will prompt any reader to ask
   who Student is. The name is unusual enough to be genuinely distracting
   without a brief note. Additionally, ν is introduced here as the degrees-of-
   freedom symbol but does not appear in notation_introduced.
   FLAGGED inline.

5. Pivoting to the CI formula — Confidence interval derivation
   The step "inverting |T| ≤ t_{α/2, n−1}" is stated but not shown. A reader
   new to CI derivation will not see how to go from the inequality to the
   interval formula. This is the conceptually hardest step in the CI section.
   FLAGGED inline.

6. Welch's test — Two-sample t-test
   Welch's test is mentioned as the software default and immediately dropped.
   A reader who uses Python or R will immediately wonder: if Welch is default,
   why was pooled just taught? A one-sentence tradeoff statement is needed.
   FLAGGED inline.

7. "Normal equations" — OLS section
   The term "normal equations" has nothing to do with the normal distribution,
   but this chapter arrives directly after a probability chapter where "normal"
   meant Gaussian. The name collision will confuse readers without a brief note.
   FLAGGED inline.

8. β̂₀ from the first normal equation — OLS derivation
   The result β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄ is presented as following from the first
   equation without showing the algebra. The step is short but requires
   distributing the sum and dividing by n.
   FLAGGED inline.

9. Pearson r vs population ρ — R² section
   r is introduced here without a formula. Readers who saw ρ in Ch 1 will
   wonder if these are the same thing. The sample/population distinction is
   not stated.
   FLAGGED inline.

10. Degrees of freedom n−2 in regression t-test
    The one-sample test used n−1; now n−2 appears. The reason (two parameters
    estimated) is not given. A reader who noticed the earlier n−1 will pause.
    FLAGGED inline.

EXERCISE CALIBRATION
Exercises are well-calibrated and cover all major chapter topics: MLE (Ex 1),
CI (Ex 2), one-sample t-test (Ex 3), two-sample t-test (Ex 4), regression
(Ex 5), ANOVA (Ex 6). The regression exercise (Ex 5) is multi-part and
substantially more work than the others; it may feel disproportionate but it
is the most important technique in the chapter and the stepper handles the
arithmetic clearly. The supplied critical values mean no tables are needed,
which is the right call for an exercise set at this layer.

WAYFINDING
"Where this goes" covers non-parametric tests, Bayesian inference, multiple
regression, and GLMs. The multiple regression mention correctly cross-references
the linear algebra section. The Bayesian inference pointer is apt: readers
who want to understand where the prior probability in Ch 1's Bayes example
comes from will find that connection satisfying. The section does not name a
specific chapter for each extension, only a direction — appropriate given that
